body:
Why defence procurement has special procedures

Government procurement is the process through which public authorities acquire goods and services. Defence procurement must consider the equipment's suitability, cost, quality, security, maintenance and long-term availability. India uses different procedures for major capital acquisitions and routine revenue purchases.

Defence Acquisition Procedure 2020

The Defence Acquisition Procedure (DAP) 2020 came into effect on 1 October 2020. It provides the framework for acquiring major defence equipment and systems under the capital expenditure head.

An important objective is to prefer indigenous design, development and manufacturing wherever appropriate. DAP 2020 gives the highest preference to the Buy (Indian-IDDM) category. IDDM means Indigenously Designed, Developed and Manufactured.

Important procurement categories

CategoryMain characteristicCore distinction
Buy (Indian-IDDM)Indigenous design, development and manufactureHighest preference under DAP 2020
Buy (Indian)Purchase from an eligible Indian vendorIndigenous design is not mandatory in every case
Buy and Make (Indian)Indian acquisition combined with subsequent domestic manufactureInvolves foreign technology transfer
Buy (Global-Manufacture in India)Foreign participation with manufacture in IndiaDomestic production need not mean indigenous original design
Buy (Global)Acquisition from eligible foreign or Indian vendors under global procurementDoes not by itself establish indigenous development

In the original DAP 2020 category provisions, Buy (Indian-IDDM) required at least 50% indigenous content, calculated on the base contract price (total contract price less taxes and duties). For Buy (Indian), the stated thresholds were at least 50% where the product had an indigenous design and at least 60% otherwise. Indigenous-content rules are subject to the applicable amendments, detailed definitions and contract conditions.

Indigenous design and indigenous content are separate tests. A product may contain many Indian-made parts but still use a foreign-origin design. Conversely, an indigenously developed system may initially depend on imported components. The applicable procurement category determines the required conditions.

Make procedures

DAP also contains arrangements for developing products domestically instead of simply purchasing a finished foreign system.

  • Make-I: Development projects involving government funding support of up to 70% of prototype development costs under DAP 2020, normally capped at ₹250 crore per development agency.
  • Make-II: Industry-funded development arrangements intended to encourage domestic innovation.
  • Make-III: Import-substitution arrangements involving indigenous manufacture of specified items.

The word Make concerns domestic development or production through a prescribed procedure. It should not be treated as proof that every underlying technology originated in India.

What does Acceptance of Necessity mean?

Acceptance of Necessity (AoN) is an in-principle approval recognising the requirement for a proposed acquisition. For relevant major proposals, the Defence Acquisition Council (DAC) considers AoN within the applicable decision-making framework.

After the necessary approvals, an acquisition may proceed through steps such as requesting proposals, technical evaluation, trials, commercial consideration and contract conclusion. The details depend on the procurement category.

A news report that the DAC has approved procurement proposals does not necessarily mean that contracts have already been signed or that the equipment has entered service.

Defence Procurement Manual 2025

The Defence Procurement Manual (DPM) 2025 became effective on 1 November 2025. It governs procurement under the revenue expenditure head, including goods and services required for the maintenance and continued functioning of existing equipment and establishments.

DocumentMain expenditure headTypical purpose
DAP 2020CapitalAcquisition of major equipment and systems
DPM 2025RevenueMaintenance, support, stores and services

Draft DAP 2026: distinguish proposals from rules

The Ministry of Defence released a draft DAP 2026 for public comments on 10 February 2026. It proposed several changes, including a higher indigenous-content requirement for the Indian-IDDM category.

The Ministry's February 2026 announcement explicitly described this document as a proposed replacement for DAP 2020, subject to approval. Therefore, the proposed 60% threshold in the draft must not be confused with the 50% benchmark originally specified for Buy (Indian-IDDM) under DAP 2020. A draft proposal does not become an operative procurement rule merely because it has been published.

Prelims focus

  • DAP 2020 became effective on 1 October 2020.
  • Buy (Indian-IDDM) receives the highest preference under DAP 2020.
  • IDDM means Indigenously Designed, Developed and Manufactured.
  • The original DAP 2020 minimum indigenous content for Buy (Indian-IDDM) was 50%.
  • DPM 2025 became effective on 1 November 2025 for revenue procurement.
  • Trap: AoN is an in-principle approval, not a signed contract or operational induction.

[Sources: Press Information Bureau, Raksha Mantri Unveils Defence Acquisition Procedure 2020, 28 September 2020, sections on acquisition categories and indigenous content; Press Information Bureau, New Procurement Policy, 4 April 2022; Press Information Bureau, Release of Defence Procurement Manual 2025, 23 October 2025; Press Information Bureau, Inviting Comments on Draft Defence Acquisition Procedure 2026, 10 February 2026; Press Information Bureau, DAP 2026 Proposes Transformative Leap, 13 February 2026. Official documents consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A flow distinguishes requirement identification, AoN approval, supplier evaluation, contract conclusion, delivery and acceptance, and operational use.
pictures.caption: Approval of a requirement is different from signing a contract or delivering equipment.

title: Defence Procurement: DAP, DPM and Indigenous Acquisition Categories

body:
Why domestic supply chains are essential

A supply chain is the network of organisations and activities required to obtain materials, produce components, assemble products and deliver them to users. A defence system depends on both its final manufacturer and the suppliers providing equipment, materials, software and maintenance support.

For example, a domestically manufactured communication system may require an antenna, electronic components, a power unit, software, a protective enclosure and testing services. Some may be supplied by Indian businesses while others are imported.

Greater domestic capability in critical components makes it easier to maintain equipment and respond when foreign supply becomes unreliable. However, building a dependable supply chain requires adequate quality, production capacity and commercially sustainable suppliers.

Import substitution

Import substitution means replacing an imported product or component with one produced domestically. It may involve an established Indian design, licensed domestic production or new research and development.

Import substitution is particularly important for spare parts and components required throughout the service life of equipment. A single unavailable component can prevent an otherwise serviceable system from functioning as intended.

Import substitution and indigenous innovation are not identical. Replacing a foreign-made part with a domestically manufactured equivalent reduces import dependence. Creating a new Indian-designed technology adds domestic research and design capability.

SRIJAN Defence Portal

The Ministry of Defence's Department of Defence Production launched the SRIJAN Defence Portal in August 2020. It allows Defence Public Sector Undertakings and Service Headquarters to identify items for which Indian industry, including MSMEs and startups, can develop domestic manufacturing capabilities.

The portal helps potential suppliers identify opportunities for import substitution. Listing an item on SRIJAN does not mean that it has already been successfully developed or that a purchase contract is guaranteed.

Positive Indigenisation Lists

Positive Indigenisation Lists (PILs) identify defence items targeted for domestic sourcing according to notified timelines. These lists help Indian industry anticipate demand and develop products previously obtained from abroad.

The import restrictions associated with listed items apply according to their prescribed conditions and timelines. A PIL does not mean that India has prohibited every defence import.

Sixth Department of Defence Production list

On 18 August 2026, the Department of Defence Production notified its 6th Positive Indigenisation List, containing 405 items. These comprised 389 DPSU items and 16 Indian Coast Guard items.

The list covered components, subsystems, spare parts and materials relevant to multiple defence platforms. Its reported estimated business potential was ₹3,070 crore. These figures describe the list as notified in August 2026; they are not figures for the entire defence industry.

Defence Industrial Corridors

The Government of India announced 2 Defence Industrial Corridors to develop manufacturing networks and attract investment. They are located in:

  • Uttar Pradesh: Agra, Aligarh, Chitrakoot, Jhansi, Kanpur and Lucknow.
  • Tamil Nadu: Chennai, Coimbatore, Hosur, Salem and Tiruchirappalli.

These corridors aim to connect manufacturers, suppliers, infrastructure and skilled labour. A defence factory can operate outside these corridors; their existence does not restrict defence production to the 2 states.

Gujarat's contribution

Gujarat is not one of the 2 centrally announced Defence Industrial Corridor states, but it has significant defence-manufacturing activity.

A notable example is the Larsen & Toubro Armoured Systems Complex at Hazira, Gujarat, which has manufactured the K9 VAJRA-T self-propelled artillery system. The Ministry of Defence reported the flagging off of the 51st K9 VAJRA-T from the Hazira complex on 16 January 2020.

This illustrates participation by private industry in Gujarat. A product manufactured in Gujarat under a technology partnership must not automatically be described as an entirely Indian-origin design.

Gandhinagar also hosted DefExpo 2022, a defence exhibition showcasing products, industrial participation and technological capabilities. Hosting an exhibition is different from being designated a Defence Industrial Corridor.

Prelims focus

  • SRIJAN Defence Portal was launched in August 2020.
  • The Department of Defence Production notified its 6th PIL on 18 August 2026.
  • The 6th DDP list included 405 items: 389 DPSU items and 16 Coast Guard items.
  • India's 2 centrally announced Defence Industrial Corridors are in Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
  • L&T's Armoured Systems Complex is located at Hazira in Gujarat.
  • Trap: Industrial activity and DefExpo events in Gujarat do not make Gujarat one of those 2 corridor states.

[Sources: NCERT, Understanding Economic Development, Class 10, Chapter 2, Sectors of the Indian Economy; Press Information Bureau, Aatmanirbhar Bharat: DDP Notifies 6th Positive Indigenisation List of 405 Items, 18 August 2026; Press Information Bureau, Defence Corridors, 11 March 2020; Press Information Bureau, Flagging Off of 51st K9 VAJRA-T Gun from L&T Armoured System Complex in Gujarat, 16 January 2020; Ministry of Defence, DefExpo 2022 event information. Official websites consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Multiple suppliers support a domestic defence product throughout its life; a missing essential part can disrupt production or maintenance.
pictures.caption: Defence manufacturing depends on a chain of material, component and specialist suppliers.

pictures.alt: Indian factory workers in safety clothing inspect a large tracked industrial vehicle inside a spacious modern manufacturing plant in Hazira, Gujarat.
pictures.caption: Modern industrial production in Gujarat contributes to India's defence-manufacturing ecosystem.

title: Defence Supply Chains, Import Substitution and Gujarat's Industrial Contribution

body:
Production and exports measure different activities

Defence production refers to the value of defence goods manufactured during a specified period under the reporting definition. Defence exports refer to defence goods and services supplied to foreign customers and recorded under the applicable export-reporting system.

These figures should not be added together to calculate national defence output. Some exported products are already included within domestic production, while reporting methods and categories may also differ.

India's defence production in FY 2025-26

According to the Ministry of Defence announcement dated 17 June 2026, the reported value of India's annual defence production reached approximately ₹1.78 lakh crore in FY 2025-26.

In that year's reported production:

  • Public-sector entities, including defence public sector undertakings and other public sector undertakings, accounted for approximately 76%.
  • Private-sector entities accounted for approximately 24%.

These percentages describe the value of production for the specified financial year. They are not the percentage of defence companies, employees, research projects or exports.

India's defence exports in FY 2025-26

On 2 April 2026, the Ministry of Defence announced defence exports of ₹38,424 crore in FY 2025-26, compared with ₹23,622 crore in FY 2024-25.

For FY 2025-26, defence public sector undertakings contributed approximately 54.84% of exports and private-sector firms approximately 45.16%.

Notice that the public-private shares of production and exports differ. The production shares were approximately 76% and 24%, while the export shares were approximately 54.84% and 45.16%. A correct statement-based question must preserve both the indicator and the financial year.

Why exports require regulation

Some defence technologies and dual-use goods can contribute to military capabilities even when sold for civilian purposes. Governments therefore regulate the export of specified sensitive items to address security obligations and prevent unauthorised transfers.

An exporter may have to establish the item's classification, the intended recipient, the end use and whether an export authorisation is required.

SCOMET: India's strategic export-control list

SCOMET stands for Special Chemicals, Organisms, Materials, Equipment and Technologies. It is India's national control list covering specified dual-use items, military goods and relevant nuclear-related items, including certain software and technologies.

SCOMET is part of India's foreign-trade control framework. The applicable authorisation requirements depend on the listed item's category and specific regulatory provisions.

AuthorityGeneral roleImportant qualification
Directorate General of Foreign TradeAuthorisations for many controlled dual-use categoriesNot the sole authority for every SCOMET item
Department of Defence ProductionAuthorisations for most Category 6 Munitions List itemsSpecific exceptions are prescribed
Department of Atomic EnergySpecified nuclear-related Category 0 controlsAdditional nuclear-transfer conditions can apply

SCOMET Category 6 is the Munitions List. The Department of Defence Production generally handles export authorisations for this category, subject to specific exceptions. DGFT handles 6A007 and 6A008, while specified military nuclear equipment is classified under Category 0 and handled by the Department of Atomic Energy. Other SCOMET categories may fall under the Directorate General of Foreign Trade or the Department of Atomic Energy.

A technology may have a lawful civilian application and still be subject to export controls. Dual-use describes possible applications; it does not mean the item is automatically free from regulation.

Three permissions that should not be confused

  • Manufacturing authorisation: Permission to manufacture an item where licensing requirements apply.
  • Technology or intellectual-property licence: Permission to use specified technical knowledge or protected rights under an agreement.
  • Export authorisation: Permission to transfer a controlled item or technology abroad when required by law.

Holding one permission does not necessarily satisfy the conditions for the others. Similarly, a product's successful testing does not automatically establish permission to export it.

Prelims focus

  • Reported defence production in FY 2025-26 was approximately ₹1.78 lakh crore.
  • Public-sector entities accounted for approximately 76% of FY 2025-26 defence production.
  • Defence exports were ₹38,424 crore in FY 2025-26, compared with ₹23,622 crore in FY 2024-25.
  • SCOMET stands for Special Chemicals, Organisms, Materials, Equipment and Technologies.
  • SCOMET Category 6 is the Munitions List.
  • Trap: A product manufactured in India is not automatically authorised for export.

[Sources: Press Information Bureau, Defence Production Soars to a Record Rs 1.78 Lakh Crore in Financial Year 2025-26, 17 June 2026; Press Information Bureau, Defence Exports Skyrocket to Record Rs 38,424 Crore in Financial Year 2025-26, 2 April 2026; Directorate General of Foreign Trade, Foreign Trade Policy 2023, Chapter 10, SCOMET provisions; DGFT, Handbook of Procedures, Chapter 10, SCOMET Categories and Licensing Jurisdiction; DGFT, Appendix 3, SCOMET List, Category 6. Official documents consulted 14 November 2026.]
